stem:
A 24-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder is stable on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily for the last 3 years after two hospitalisations for mania in her early 20s. She and her new partner have started discussing having a baby in the next 12 months. She currently uses no contraception and denies missed periods. Prior trials of lithium caused unacceptable tremor and cognitive slowing, and olanzapine caused significant weight gain. She has never been trialled on lamotrigine.

On examination she is euthymic with good insight. She has no active suicidal ideation. She is well engaged with her community mental health team. Her most recent valproate level was 550 micromol/L (300-700), FBC, LFTs and pregnancy test today are normal. She reads widely and asks specifically about the risks of continuing valproate through pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74/min, blood pressure 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Euthymic, good insight, no suicidal or homicidal ideation
data_table.Investigations: Valproate 550 micromol/L (300-700); full blood count within normal limits; liver function tests within normal limits; beta hCG negative today

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Continue valproate at current dose through pregnancy because the mood benefits outweigh teratogenic risk for a stable patient
options.rationale: Valproate has a 10 percent rate of major congenital malformations and up to 40 percent rate of neurodevelopmental effects; continuation through planned pregnancy is not consistent with TGA and RANZCP guidance. (Source: TGA Valproate and Pregnancy)

options.text: Halve valproate dose to 500 mg daily immediately to reduce dose-dependent teratogenicity and continue conception planning
options.rationale: Lower valproate doses reduce but do not eliminate teratogenic risk; dose reduction alone is inadequate. (Source: TGA Valproate and Pregnancy)

options.text: Add 5 mg folate daily and continue valproate through the first trimester to reduce neural tube defect risk
options.rationale: High-dose folate is recommended alongside valproate but does not offset the teratogenic risk profile of the drug itself; valproate substitution is the priority. (Source: TGA Valproate and Pregnancy)

options.text: Ensure reliable contraception, plan cross-titration to lamotrigine before conception, and start 5 mg folate daily
options.rationale: Valproate in a woman of childbearing potential requires effective contraception and consideration of a safer alternative such as lamotrigine before conception; folate 5 mg daily is added periconception. (Source: TGA Valproate and Pregnancy)

options.text: Cease valproate abruptly today and monitor mood over the next 4 to 6 weeks without any bridging medication or plan
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation risks manic relapse; cross-titration to lamotrigine (or alternative) is safer than washout. (Source: TGA Valproate and Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Sodium valproate is highly teratogenic: around 10 percent risk of major congenital malformations (neural tube defects, cardiac, craniofacial, limb) and up to 40 percent risk of neurodevelopmental effects including autism spectrum disorder. TGA and RANZCP guidance requires reliable contraception for all women of childbearing potential on valproate; a pregnancy prevention program with documented shared decision-making should be in place. When pregnancy is planned or possible, cross-titrate to a safer alternative (lamotrigine for bipolar maintenance, lithium as second-line, olanzapine short-term). Folate 5 mg daily is recommended if valproate cannot be stopped (higher than the standard 0.5 mg periconception dose). Any discovered pregnancy on valproate warrants urgent specialist review.
key_points: Valproate has 10 percent major malformation risk and up to 40 percent neurodevelopmental risk.
Reliable contraception required for all women of childbearing potential.
Cross-titrate to lamotrigine before planned conception where possible.
5 mg daily folate if valproate cannot be stopped.
explanation.pearls: Sodium valproate has around 10 percent major malformation and up to 40 percent neurodevelopmental risk; substitute to lamotrigine before planned conception and use 5 mg daily folate periconception.

sources.label: RANZCP Bipolar Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline

stem:
You are the emergency registrar. A 38-year-old woman is brought in by ambulance 90 minutes after ingesting an unknown quantity of amitriptyline. Her partner found her drowsy at home with an empty 100-tablet 25 mg blister pack of amitriptyline that was previously two-thirds full. Paramedics report she had a brief self-terminating seizure en route. She takes no other medications.

On arrival she is drowsy with a GCS of 12 (E3 V4 M5). Pupils are mid-dilated and sluggish. Skin is warm and dry. Bladder is palpable. Her ECG on arrival shows sinus tachycardia at 132/min, QRS 140 ms, terminal R wave in aVR, QTc 480 ms. Venous blood gas shows pH 7.26, pCO2 44 mmHg, HCO3 19 mmol/L, lactate 3.2 mmol/L (0.5-2.2). She is peripherally cool with a delayed capillary refill.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 132/min, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 37.2 degrees C
data_table.Examination: GCS 12 (E3 V4 M5), mid-dilated sluggish pupils, warm dry skin, palpable bladder, cool peripheries
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus tachycardia 132/min, QRS 140 ms, terminal R wave in aVR, QTc 480 ms; VBG pH 7.26, pCO2 44, HCO3 19, lactate 3.2 mmol/L (0.5-2.2)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial pharmacological intervention?

options.text: Administer intravenous flumazenil 200 microgram to reverse suspected benzodiazepine co-ingestion contributing to sedation
options.rationale: Flumazenil is contraindicated in mixed overdose because it lowers the seizure threshold; the picture here is TCA toxicity. (Source: Australian Poisons Information Centre TCA Overdose)
source_refs: Australian Poisons Information Centre TCA Overdose

options.text: Give amiodarone 300 mg intravenously over 20 minutes for QRS widening with tachyarrhythmia and impending arrest
options.rationale: Class III antiarrhythmics prolong QT and worsen sodium channel blockade; they are contraindicated in TCA toxicity. (Source: Australian Poisons Information Centre TCA Overdose)
source_refs: Australian Poisons Information Centre TCA Overdose

options.text: Commence noradrenaline infusion at 0.05 microgram per kilogram per minute for hypotension without alkalinising therapy
options.rationale: Vasopressor may be needed adjunctively but the primary intervention for QRS widening and hypotension in TCA overdose is sodium bicarbonate. (Source: Australian Poisons Information Centre TCA Overdose)
source_refs: Australian Poisons Information Centre TCA Overdose

options.text: Give oral activated charcoal 50 g via nasogastric tube now for gastrointestinal decontamination as first priority
options.rationale: Charcoal is of low value beyond 1-2 hours after ingestion and risks aspiration in a drowsy patient; sodium bicarbonate takes priority. (Source: Australian Poisons Information Centre TCA Overdose)
source_refs: Australian Poisons Information Centre TCA Overdose

options.text: Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol per kilogram bolus targeting pH 7.5 and QRS narrowing
options.rationale: QRS above 100 ms with terminal R in aVR indicates significant sodium channel blockade; sodium bicarbonate bolus reverses toxicity via alkalinisation and sodium loading. (Source: Australian Poisons Information Centre TCA Overdose)
source_refs: Australian Poisons Information Centre TCA Overdose

explanation.summary: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose causes anticholinergic delirium, sodium channel blockade (widened QRS, terminal R in aVR, ventricular arrhythmia), potassium channel blockade (prolonged QTc), alpha blockade (hypotension) and seizures. Sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol/kg intravenous bolus is the mainstay for cardiovascular toxicity: it alkalinises to reduce free drug binding to sodium channels and provides a sodium load to overcome channel blockade, targeting arterial pH 7.45-7.55 and QRS narrowing. Seizures are treated with benzodiazepines; noradrenaline is preferred for refractory hypotension despite alkalinisation, and Class Ia, Ic and III antiarrhythmics are contraindicated. Charcoal is only of value within around 1 hour of ingestion in an alert patient with a protected airway.
key_points: QRS above 100 ms plus terminal R in aVR indicates significant TCA sodium channel blockade.
Sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol/kg bolus is first-line for cardiovascular toxicity.
Target arterial pH 7.45-7.55 and QRS narrowing.
Class Ia, Ic and III antiarrhythmics are contraindicated.
explanation.pearls: In TCA overdose with QRS above 100 ms or terminal R in aVR, give sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol/kg intravenous bolus targeting arterial pH 7.5 and QRS narrowing.

sources.label: Australian Poisons Information Centre TCA Overdose

subtopic_detail: Schizoaffective disorder vs bipolar I with psychotic features
stem:
You are the community psychiatry registrar reviewing a 26-year-old man for a diagnostic clarification. Over the last 3 years he has had three admissions. The first was for a manic episode with grandiose delusions and severe overspending, lasting 8 weeks, with delusions resolving as mood stabilised on lithium and olanzapine. The second was a severe depressive episode with psychomotor retardation and mood-congruent nihilistic delusions, resolving with ECT and antidepressant. The third, six months ago, was for two weeks of persecutory delusions and auditory hallucinations occurring in the setting of euthymic mood and no sleep or energy changes, resolving on aripiprazole.

Between episodes he has been employed part time as a barista, socially engaged with friends, and adherent to olanzapine 10 mg with lithium 900 mg. His mother has bipolar I disorder. He denies substance use and a urine drug screen has consistently been negative. There are no autism spectrum, developmental or intellectual disability features. Insight into the illness is good.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Currently euthymic, no active psychotic symptoms, good insight
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative on multiple occasions; TFT, UEC and lithium level within normal limits

lead_in: Which single diagnosis best explains his clinical course?

options.text: Schizoaffective disorder bipolar type based on the presence of psychotic symptoms without concurrent mood disturbance
options.rationale: The DSM-5 discriminator between schizoaffective disorder and bipolar with psychotic features is the presence of psychotic symptoms for at least 2 weeks in the absence of a major mood episode; his third admission meets this criterion. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Bipolar I disorder with psychotic features that only occur during mood episodes across all presentations
options.rationale: Bipolar I with psychotic features requires the psychosis to occur exclusively during mood episodes; his third admission was psychosis with euthymic mood, which excludes this diagnosis. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Schizophrenia with concurrent depressive symptoms and comorbid mood-related admissions but no true bipolarity
options.rationale: Schizophrenia requires 6 months of continuous illness with predominant psychotic features; his baseline function and episodic course argue against this. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Substance-induced psychotic disorder because acute psychotic episodes commonly follow cannabis or amphetamine use
options.rationale: Multiple negative urine drug screens and no substance use history exclude a substance-induced disorder. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Delusional disorder because persecutory delusions occurred without hallucinations or mood disturbance in the third episode
options.rationale: Delusional disorder excludes prominent hallucinations; he has had auditory hallucinations, and his prior mood episodes exclude the diagnosis. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

explanation.summary: Schizoaffective disorder is diagnosed when psychotic symptoms (delusions, hallucinations) persist for at least 2 weeks in the absence of a major mood episode across the lifetime course of illness, in a patient who also meets criteria for a major mood episode (major depression, mania or mixed) concurrent with symptoms meeting criterion A of schizophrenia. Subtypes are bipolar (manic or mixed episodes have occurred) and depressive (only major depressive episodes). Distinguishing it from bipolar with psychotic features (psychosis only during mood episodes) and from schizophrenia (mood symptoms brief and secondary) is often only possible after several episodes. Treatment combines mood stabiliser with antipsychotic; response to lithium is typically less robust than in bipolar disorder alone.
key_points: Schizoaffective disorder requires 2+ weeks of psychosis without mood episode.
Bipolar with psychotic features has psychosis only during mood episodes.
Longitudinal history over multiple episodes is required for accurate diagnosis.
Treatment combines mood stabiliser with antipsychotic.
explanation.pearls: The DSM-5-TR discriminator between schizoaffective disorder and bipolar with psychotic features is at least 2 weeks of psychosis without a concurrent major mood episode.

stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar assessing a 19-year-old man on the acute mental health inpatient unit day 3 post-admission. He was brought by police 3 days ago after climbing a construction crane in central Melbourne responding to voices telling him to warn the city about surveillance. His mother reports daily heavy use of high-potency skunk cannabis for the past 2 years and heavier use in the fortnight before admission after his relationship ended. Urine drug screen on admission was positive for cannabinoids only; alcohol, amphetamines and cocaine were negative.

On assessment today he remains suspicious with fleeting thought disorder and continuing third-person auditory hallucinations that he describes as the same voices as in the community. Sleep and mood are unremarkable. He has no personal or family psychiatric history. Since admission he has abstained from cannabis (verified by nursing observation and repeat negative urine drug screen 48 hours ago) and has received one dose of olanzapine 10 mg on admission but nothing since due to being suspicious of medication.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84/min, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert but suspicious, thought disorder present, persistent third-person auditory hallucinations, no formal thought insertion or withdrawal
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen admission cannabinoids only; repeat drug screen 48 hours ago negative for all substances; FBC, UEC, TSH within normal limits

lead_in: Which of the following best guides the next diagnostic step?

options.text: Diagnose primary schizophrenia now and commence long-acting injectable paliperidone as maintenance therapy today
options.rationale: Schizophrenia requires 6 months of continuous symptoms with 1 month of active phase; declaring the diagnosis before observing symptom trajectory off cannabis is premature. (Source: RANZCP Substance-Induced Psychotic Disorders Guidance)

options.text: Continue observation and reassess psychotic symptoms after 1 month of confirmed abstinence to clarify diagnosis
options.rationale: Substance-induced psychotic disorder typically resolves within 1 month of abstinence; persistence beyond that period supports a primary diagnosis. (Source: RANZCP Substance-Induced Psychotic Disorders Guidance)

options.text: Discharge home now with cannabis harm reduction advice and community mental health follow up in the next 2 weeks
options.rationale: He remains actively psychotic and command hallucinations previously led to dangerous behaviour; discharge is unsafe. (Source: RANZCP Substance-Induced Psychotic Disorders Guidance)

options.text: Request magnetic resonance imaging of brain today to exclude organic cause as an exclusion diagnosis step
options.rationale: Neuroimaging is not routinely required for first episode psychosis in a young person without focal neurology; observation off substance is more informative. (Source: RANZCP Substance-Induced Psychotic Disorders Guidance)

options.text: Commence clozapine now for cannabis-induced psychosis that is not responding to a standard antipsychotic trial
options.rationale: Clozapine is reserved for treatment resistance after two adequate trials of other antipsychotics; he has not had an adequate first trial. (Source: RANZCP Substance-Induced Psychotic Disorders Guidance)

explanation.summary: Distinguishing substance-induced from primary psychotic disorder in a young person with heavy cannabis use is often only possible longitudinally. DSM-5-TR criteria for substance-induced psychotic disorder require symptoms developing during or soon after intoxication or withdrawal, symptoms attributable to the substance based on temporal course and pharmacology, and symptoms not better explained by an independent psychotic disorder (e.g. onset before substance use, persistence beyond 1 month of abstinence). Cannabis is a known risk factor for later schizophrenia, particularly with early-onset heavy use of high-potency cannabis. Management is safe containment during acute presentation, antipsychotic if symptoms persist, monitored abstinence, and formal reassessment at around 1 month.
key_points: Substance-induced psychosis typically resolves within 1 month of abstinence.
Persistence beyond 1 month supports a primary psychotic disorder diagnosis.
Cannabis is a risk factor for later schizophrenia, especially with early heavy use.
Management is antipsychotic and abstinence; clozapine only after two failed trials.
explanation.pearls: Cannabis-induced psychotic disorder typically resolves within 1 month of abstinence; persistence beyond that supports a primary schizophrenia spectrum diagnosis.

stem:
You are the consultation-liaison psychiatry registrar called to the medical ward to review a 45-year-old woman with schizoaffective disorder admitted 5 days ago with reduced oral intake and mutism. Her long-term outpatient team titrated up her olanzapine from 10 to 20 mg over the last month for worsening psychosis. Since admission she has become progressively less responsive; today she has not eaten, spoken or moved.

On examination she is alert with eyes tracking, mute, and lies rigid on the bed with waxy flexibility of the arms and echolalia when addressed loudly. Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale is 16 (over 3 features present). Her temperature is 37.1 degrees C. Creatine kinase is 380 U/L (30-200), white cell count 8.4 x10^9/L, no autonomic instability, and no lead-pipe rigidity. She has no history of NMS. Her mother had major depressive disorder with a similar presentation years ago that responded to ECT.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 37.1 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Mute, waxy flexibility both arms, echolalia when addressed, no lead-pipe rigidity, no clonus, no autonomic instability
data_table.Investigations: Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale 16; creatine kinase 380 U/L (30-200); WCC 8.4 x10^9/L; urea and electrolytes within normal limits; CT head within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate diagnostic and therapeutic step now?

options.text: Cease olanzapine and commence bromocriptine 2.5 mg twice daily for suspected neuroleptic malignant syndrome
options.rationale: NMS features are absent: no hyperthermia, no lead-pipe rigidity, no autonomic instability and only mildly elevated CK; the picture is catatonia. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Practice Guidance)

options.text: Continue olanzapine, add haloperidol 5 mg intramuscular for behavioural containment and monitor response
options.rationale: High-potency antipsychotics can precipitate malignant catatonia and NMS in this setting and are contraindicated. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Practice Guidance)

options.text: Administer intravenous lorazepam 2 mg as a diagnostic-therapeutic challenge, watching for improvement in 15-30 min
options.rationale: The lorazepam challenge (1-2 mg IV) is both diagnostic and therapeutic for catatonia; typical improvement within 15-30 minutes confirms the diagnosis and starts treatment. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Practice Guidance)

options.text: Refer directly for electroconvulsive therapy within the next 24 hours without any pharmacological challenge trial
options.rationale: ECT is highly effective but is typically reserved for lorazepam-refractory catatonia or malignant catatonia; a lorazepam challenge is the first step. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Practice Guidance)

options.text: Trial oral fluoxetine 20 mg for underlying depressive stupor and observe for 7 days before further intervention
options.rationale: SSRIs are ineffective for catatonic stupor; benzodiazepine or ECT is the standard approach. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Practice Guidance)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is diagnosed when at least 3 of 12 features are present on the DSM-5-TR or Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale: stupor, catalepsy, waxy flexibility, mutism, negativism, posturing, mannerism, stereotypy, agitation, grimacing, echolalia, echopraxia. Causes include primary psychiatric disorders (schizophrenia, mood disorders), medical or neurological conditions and medications. A 1-2 mg intravenous lorazepam challenge is both diagnostic and therapeutic: rapid partial response confirms the diagnosis. Treatment is scheduled oral or intravenous lorazepam titrated to response, with ECT reserved for lorazepam-refractory cases or malignant catatonia (autonomic instability, hyperthermia). Antipsychotics can worsen or precipitate malignant catatonia and NMS.
key_points: 3+ features on DSM-5-TR or Bush-Francis criteria establishes catatonia.
Lorazepam 1-2 mg IV is both diagnostic and therapeutic.
ECT is used for lorazepam-refractory or malignant catatonia.
Avoid high-potency antipsychotics which can worsen the picture.
explanation.pearls: In catatonia, give intravenous lorazepam 1-2 mg as a diagnostic-therapeutic challenge and expect partial response in 15-30 minutes; avoid high-potency antipsychotics which risk precipitating malignant catatonia.

subtopic_detail: Endocarditis modified Duke criteria and empirical antibiotic
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 68-year-old woman on the acute medical unit with 3 weeks of malaise, unintentional 3 kg weight loss, drenching night sweats and a low grade fever. She had a bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement 4 years ago for severe calcific aortic stenosis. She has no intravenous drug use history and no recent dental work. She lives in inner Perth.

On examination she is unwell but not septic. There is a soft ejection systolic murmur in the aortic area unchanged from her clinic notes and a new small area of petechiae on her right conjunctiva; no other embolic signs and no splinter haemorrhages. Chest is clear. Abdomen is soft with no tenderness. Two sets of blood cultures taken 12 hours apart both grow Streptococcus sanguinis, and a transthoracic echocardiogram today shows a 6 mm vegetation on the bioprosthetic aortic valve leaflet with mild valvular regurgitation. She has no penicillin allergy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, blood pressure 122/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 38.1 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Soft ejection systolic murmur aortic area, small right conjunctival petechial patch, no splinter haemorrhages, no splenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Two sets of blood cultures 12 hours apart both positive for Streptococcus sanguinis; transthoracic echocardiogram 6 mm vegetation on bioprosthetic aortic valve with mild regurgitation; CRP 82 mg/L (<10); WCC 10.4 x10^9/L; creatinine 78 micromol/L

lead_in: Which regimen best meets Australian empirical treatment for her prosthetic valve endocarditis while susceptibilities are pending?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily with rifampicin 300 mg twice daily as an outpatient management plan
options.rationale: Prosthetic valve endocarditis requires prolonged intravenous therapy; oral is not appropriate for empirical treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Infective Endocarditis)

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.8 g every 4 hours as monotherapy for a total treatment duration of 6 weeks
options.rationale: Prosthetic valve viridans strep endocarditis requires combination therapy with an aminoglycoside and gentamicin for the first 2 weeks. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Infective Endocarditis)

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin 25 mg per kilogram every 12 hours plus rifampicin 600 mg oral twice daily for 6 weeks
options.rationale: Vancomycin plus rifampicin is used for Staphylococcus aureus prosthetic valve endocarditis with penicillin allergy; not first-line for viridans strep. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Infective Endocarditis)

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.8 g every 4 hours plus gentamicin 1 mg per kilogram every 8 hours for 2 weeks
options.rationale: Viridans streptococcal prosthetic valve endocarditis is treated with 6 weeks of penicillin plus 2 weeks of synergistic gentamicin per Therapeutic Guidelines. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Infective Endocarditis)

options.text: Intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g every 4 hours plus gentamicin 1 mg per kilogram every 8 hours
options.rationale: Flucloxacillin covers staphylococci and is not the drug of choice for viridans streptococcal endocarditis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Infective Endocarditis)

explanation.summary: Infective endocarditis is diagnosed by the modified Duke criteria: definite endocarditis requires 2 major, or 1 major and 3 minor, or 5 minor criteria. Major criteria are typical organisms in 2 separate blood cultures plus evidence of endocardial involvement on imaging (vegetation, abscess, new regurgitation, prosthetic dehiscence). Native valve viridans streptococcal endocarditis is treated with 4 weeks of penicillin or ceftriaxone, or 2 weeks combined with gentamicin. Prosthetic valve viridans streptococcal endocarditis is treated with 6 weeks of penicillin plus 2 weeks of gentamicin; surgery is indicated for heart failure, uncontrolled infection, large vegetation, abscess or prosthetic dehiscence.
key_points: Two positive blood cultures with typical organism plus echo evidence = definite endocarditis.
Prosthetic viridans strep endocarditis: penicillin 6 weeks plus gentamicin 2 weeks.
Native viridans strep endocarditis: penicillin 4 weeks or penicillin plus gentamicin 2 weeks.
Surgical indications include heart failure, uncontrolled infection, large vegetation, abscess.
explanation.pearls: Prosthetic valve viridans streptococcal endocarditis in Australia is treated with 6 weeks of intravenous benzylpenicillin plus synergistic gentamicin for the first 2 weeks.
